title: Precious Is Just a Label
question: What makes one gemstone precious and another not?
hook: Amethyst was counted as a precious stone for centuries, until large amounts of it turned up in Brazil.
idea: The precious label grew from ancient rarity and quality, so it does not always match what a gem is worth today.

beats.prompt: Sort each gemstone into its traditional group
beats.explain: In modern use only emerald, ruby, sapphire and diamond are precious; every other gemstone, including garnet and lapis lazuli, is semi-precious.

beats.prompt: A stone long ranked as precious is suddenly found in bulk. What happened to its precious status in the case of amethyst?

choices.label: It stayed precious, since tradition is fixed
choices.feedback: Tradition sounds permanent, but amethyst's ranking did not survive the new supply.

choices.label: It lost its place among precious stones
It became more precious as more people wore it
choices.feedback: Popularity helped some stones, but amethyst's ranking ended with the Brazilian discoveries.

beats.explain: Amethyst counted as precious until bulk amethyst was found in Brazil in the 19th century, suggesting rarity played a part in the label.

beats.prompt: Match each title to who or what it names
pairs: An old term for semi-precious gems
beats.explain: The gem trade has its own names for experts, cutters and older categories of stone.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: Emerald is one of the four precious stones.
Garnet is counted as a semi-precious stone.
A precious stone is always worth more than a semi-precious one.
So any emerald is worth more than any garnet.
beats.explain: The traditional split does not necessarily reflect market value: the green garnet tsavorite can be far more valuable than a mid-quality emerald.
